utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would, in any event, like to continue to cross-examine the witness. We are very sorry that the witness was upset obviously. Her story is a very hard one, but we have the statement which the witness gave to the investigators of the OTP on the 4th of May, 2001, in which gives us a completely different story. And my questions were going in the same direction as she spoke. I didn't think that I would upset her, but I need some minutes more to cross-examine her because they are so glaringly inconsistent with what she said in the statement. She even spoke about the army in this statement. So it's very inconsistent with what she said today. Tomorrow my co-counsel will ask her a couple of questions, tomorrow if she can not come today. Of course we have to bear in mind the present state in which the witness is, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, by my rough notes I spent 29 minutes in examination-in-chief, and the Defence had spent approximately 18 minutes until the time we broke, and I just was wanted to point out that if my learned colleague had very important matters to cross-examine the witness, they had an opportunity to begin with that. And I am not saying that the cross-examination should be curtailed by any means, but simply pointing out the time period that has been allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that brings us in a situation. I have been informed that we cannot continue at this very moment. That would mean that very much depends on how the situation will be tomorrow morning, and of course we have to face the potential situation that General Galic will not be available in the courtroom, and therefore we cannot continue since General Galic has expressed his wish to be present. That would also mean that the witness would have to stay over the weekend since we are not sitting on Friday. She would have to stay at least until next Monday, and we also have the problem that the holiday on Friday is an important one especially for the -- for the witness. So I wonder whether we could find a solution for this last 10 minutes, either by General Galic agreeing upon just this witness to be cross-examined tomorrow for 10 minutes in his absence, or... Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps a completely different solution, Mr. President, one that's not normal with respect to this trial and the way this Trial Chamber has proceeded. But if the Defence's position is that there are numerous contradictions in her statement, perhaps one way would be to simply admit her entire statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would be the position as far as the -- do I understand from your reaction that it's -- especially on the basis of the statement that you would like to cross-examine her?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. And what about the potential situation if we would continue tomorrow morning, even if it would be for a short period of time when General Galic is not present? And I'll not change any decision of yesterday, but if he would change his mind just for this one witness for 10 minutes or a quarter of a an hour or 20 minutes, then I would like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, we would like to talk to our client. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if it happens that General Galic cannot be present here at 9.00 because he is having -- because of the medical examination, then the General agrees that those 10 or 15 minutes of cross-examination of the witness, in view of her health, be done in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thank not only the Defence, but also General Galic for this understanding of the position of the witness. So that would mean, Mr. Mundis, that we could now continue with the examination-in-chief of the next witness, and tomorrow morning we could -- at the appropriate time, we could continue the cross-examination of Witness Jusovic. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Assuming her medical condition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. And if not, we are in a totally different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In that event, Mr. President, the Prosecution calls Naza Ocuz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd just like to put a question to the interpreters' booth, if I split up the solemn declaration in four parts as far as the translation is concerned, can you follow the split up in these four parts?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We shall do our best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll explain it to you. The English text leaves an opportunity to split up the solemn declaration in four parts, but I don't know whether this would be a problem for the translators to follow that splitting up. We'll see what happens. You're Naza Ocuz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am Ocuz, Nazija, born in 1946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, very well. I can understand everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Ocuz, before you will testify in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Do I understand well that you cannot read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see to read, but I will speak from the bottom of my heart, and I will be speaking the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then, please, repeat my words and say the following: "I solemnly declare."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "That I will speak the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The whole truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "And nothing but the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mrs. Ocuz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, will you please tell the Trial Chamber in what city you reside?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: In Sedrenik, Sarajevo, Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I've lived there for 50 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did the war start in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: In 1992, in April. 5th or 6th of April. I'm old, so I think so. I remember the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a result of the war beginning in Sedrenik, did your life change?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, a great deal. A great deal. Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us how life changed for you once the war started?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: It changed. It was not possible to go anywhere, nowhere, absolutely nowhere. We could not walk anywhere. Day changed for night. We could not walk. We couldn't go anywhere. So that's how I remember it in my locality where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "day changed for night," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: We could not walk or move about or work during the day because of the sniping, because of shells. We just had to stay in the cellar sheltering, taking cover, hidden. If you try to walk out during the day, then you would be hit. You would be injured. There would be no more you, either wounded or dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, approximately how long did you stay in the cellar during each day?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Throughout every day. My husband was sick. I had to look after him. I had to -- I had to do everything during the day. We would dig, we would sew, we would go and fetch the water. We did everything during the day. We would fetch the water. We would do it, sorry, during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where would you go to fetch the water?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Not very far, quite close. It's a reservoir. Everybody knows in Sarajevo where that is, reservoir. We went at night. There was a queue. People would go and sleep there waiting for their turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go to collect firewood for heating or cooking purposes?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Just above the reservoir. Well, there are several reservoirs. There was the whole wood was cut down because we needed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The area where you cut wood, do you know the name of that area?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: It's called Pasino Brdo. I just remembered, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In order to protect your house from the snipers that you've testified about, did you make any changes or modifications to your house in order to protect yourselves?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, with my son we put bricks up. My husband was sick. He couldn't do it. So we put bricks. They were red, red bricks. We put them up. We had to put them all one on top of the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you put these bricks in the windows?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did. Yes, just the windows from the dangerous side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which side was the "dangerous side" of your house?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Everybody knows that. It was Spicesta, Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why was Spicasta Stijena a dangerous place?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Because the Serb army was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know which government or armed force controlled the area of Sedrenik where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that. I don't know anything about that. During the day, I never went out. I wasn't interested. I was just trying to keep my child's life, my own, my husband's, and my husband got very sick, and now he is no more. So I remained by myself to suffer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, take your time. If you feel -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we are aware that it will all be very emotional.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the latter part of 1992 and during the year of 1993, was the Sedrenik area of Sarajevo targeted by snipers?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They fired, and even at night. They even had night weapons. They fired at night. And I can tell you that they fired at the woman. She was turning over. I won't tell her name. She was turning, and they fired, and she said they could see me as if it was daytime. I don't want to tell her name. If somebody needs her name, they can look for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what time period it was that this woman was shot?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: It was night. I don't remember the dates. I don't remember the dates. There was -- it was terrible. It was...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, in addition to the bricks that you placed over your windows, did you also use a form of plastic to cover the windows?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We got -- from humanitarian help we got plastic to protect ourselves from the cold, from the bullets, from the snipers. So we tried to protect ourselves because we did not everything -- we did not have enough of things to we had to give things to each other to protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the glass in your windows intact during 1993?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no. It was a nylon foil, plastic foil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why were there no window panes in the windows during 1993?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Of course the shrapnel broke it all. It's all broken. Yes, all the windows are broken, so the foil is the only thing we had to protect ourselves, as much as it could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you wounded by a sniper, Mrs. Ocuz, during the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In 1993, I'll never forget that. I'll never forget that day as long as I live. We set lunch, we were going to have lunch, my son and I. And my kuma was out in the street, and I said to my son -- my neighbour was out in the street. And I said to my son, can you hear the firing, can you feel the firing? My son said, "No, no." I said I was hurt and I didn't want him to approach me because -- so we went to call the neighbour for help. It was terrible. So my son went to the door, and I said, "please come back." And then they took me into the car. Then I -- immediately they operated on me. I was 15 days in the hospital. And after that, after the bandages, I had a cast. I had regular checkups, whenever the doctor said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In what part of your house were you located at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: On the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which room?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: In the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the kitchen have a window that faced Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did. Yes, both from the room and the kitchen and on the first floor and the upstairs as well, they were both facing that way towards the Spicasta Stijena. All the windows were facing that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like you to focus on the window that was in the kitchen. At the time you were shot, was that window covered by bricks and plastic?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we had put the bricks there, and my son as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the bricks cover the window entirely, or was there still an opening in the bricks to allow light to come in?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no. No, light could not come in. No, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you see from your kitchen Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, only if I went out at night, then I could see it. I could see where the -- where the evil was coming from on to my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you -- you were in your kitchen at the time that you were shot. What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes. I was having lunch. I just sat down to have lunch. My son was on my left-hand side. I was on the right. And my husband always said, "don't sit there. Whoever sit there -- I said don't sit on that side because the bullet will hit you." He is not there. He is dead, my husband, but I am telling you the truth what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time you were shot, were you, in fact, sitting in the location that your husband had warned you about?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, on that side, yes. Not quite at the place, but on that side. On the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In what part of your body did the bullet hit you?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: A lower leg, in the bone, shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this on your left leg or your right leg?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry, but I believe what is interpreted by the French booth is not what is in the English transcript. I believe that I heard in the French translation that the husband was bearing a rifle, that he knew these technical questions. And it doesn't seem to come out at all in the English transcript. This doesn't appear in the transcript as I am reading it in 73, line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is true that nothing appears in the English translation on any issue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin has just confronted us with. It seems to be different than the French translation. Could perhaps the French booth inform me about what is exactly in reference to translation. We are talking about page 73, line 12. I don't know whether the interpreters also can follow the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, none of the booths can follow the French screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The French booth informs me that to the best of their recollection, the husband had been -- carried arms before, and therefore knew what he was talking about. Is that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what is in your -- well, at least we established that there might have been a translation problem. I think we have now heard both the text without this phrase, and we have this phrase explained by the French booth. If one of the parties thinks it of vital importance, of course we'll have to check the original language used, and then see whether the transcripts are in need of any redaction in this respect. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis. Mrs. Ocuz, we just had to pay a bit of attention to the translation of what you have said. It is translated in two languages, and there seemed to be a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- But we now continue, and we can now concentrate again on what is important, that is, your story. Please, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, you said a few moments ago that you were wounded in the bone of your leg. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Right leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In your right leg. Was this the upper part of your leg or the lower part of your leg?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Lower part of my leg. Above the ankle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you went to the hospital, and that you stayed there for about 15 days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you returned to your house, did you examine the kitchen walls to see where the bullet might have come from?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes. I examined, and I saw there was a bullet in the foil. There were three parts of the window, and it was the middle part of the window. It had a hole, so this is where the bullet had entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say foil, was this the plastic foil that the humanitarian aid agency distributed to you?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, when you left the hospital, did they give you some paperwork, some documents?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At a later time when you were interviewed by an investigator from the Tribunal, did you then provide those medical documents to that investigator?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did that investigator also ask you to sign those medical records on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I know you mentioned earlier that your eyesight wasn't too good, but if I were to show you that document, do you think you would recognise your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, yes, large letters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown the document marked P1716, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This is the document that you gave to the investigator of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this is the document that the hospital gave you when you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, this is the very same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Ocuz. I'd like to ask you now a few questions about some of your neighbours. Do you know Mejra Jusovic?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know her well. I know she is my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, did you frequently go with Mrs. Jusovic to collect wood in Pasino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All of the neighbours, friends went at night to get the wood. But mostly with Mejra.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, how often would you go with Mejra Jusovic to collect wood?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't count the times, but I often went with her. I often went with Mejra. I didn't count the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you ever with Mejra Jusovic when a sniper fired at the two of you?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you ever with Mejra Jusovic when she was grazed by a bullet?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember what year or date that was when that happened?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no. I don't remember the date. I don't remember the year. I don't remember that. I only remember my own, my own leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the period from 1992 through 1993 and into 1994, did you ever see any heavy military equipment or military weapons in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, nothing. I did not see anything. If there was it during daytime, I don't know because I never left the cellar. I did not go Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. anywhere. At daytime, we would sleep. You would cook in the cellar, and then at night, we had to fetch the wood, get the wood, do the laundry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any military weapons or heavy military equipment on Pasino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no. When would I go there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any soldiers on Pasino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, on Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But not on Pasino Brdo in the area where you collected wood?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mejra Jusovic wearing any kind of military uniform?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see her carrying -- did you ever see her carrying any kind of military weapon or rifle or gun of any kind?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No. No, the only thing I know, it was wood. Mejra and I would just carry wood. We were always in civilian, old trousers, just rags really, whatever we wore -- whatever we had, we wore. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever wear a military uniform, Mrs. Ocuz?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And finally, during 1993, do you know of other neighbours or friends of yours who lived in Sedrenik who were the victims of sniping or shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. A neighbourhood was killed there. Another neighbour was wounded there. If I could write, I would write a book of all the people who had been wounded. But whatever remains in my soul, that's what I can tell you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And these people who were killed and wounded, do you know what year or years they were killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the years. During the war, you know how long it went on for, for four years. Everyone was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these people that were killed and wounded, killed or wounded around the same time, within a few months of the time that you were wounded in the war?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No. This day, that day, one was wounded, one was killed, one was wounded, one was killed. It just happened that way. How can I know the dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This period of people being killed and wounded, it extended throughout the war, from middle 1992 through 1994? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Ocuz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Mrs. Ocuz, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic, you're ready to cross-examine the witness? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Ocuz.

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, can you confirm for us that on the 20th of September, 2001, you gave a statement to OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't remember days. Believe me, I don't remember any days.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But was it in 2001?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, was it during the last summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Last summer. Yes, yes, quite right. Last summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, can you tell us, before you gave this statement in the summer of 2001, did you report the incident that you told us about today?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Which incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that you were wounded, and did you report it to the police or some other authority in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I see. Well, I guess my son reported it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how old is your son?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: He was 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And before the summer of 2001, did you give any statement to any authority about the incident, or was this the first time?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone, except those foreigners who came and asked me. That's what I know, and I'm telling the truth. They came and asked me about how I received my wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you lived with your son and husband.

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if your son and husband prior to the conflict in Sarajevo were fulltime employed?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, my son was fulltime employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where he worked?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: He worked for Granap.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what about your husband?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: He was ill. I already told you, in 1996, in the winter, he --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But did he work before he fell ill?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: He was retired. He worked for self-employed, entrepreneur, then he was retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you employed?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: In a Medresa.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you work during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to the house that you lived in, precisely Sedrenik, can you tell us precisely what street? Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Sedrenik Street. That's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does your house have a number?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, it has a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And it is which?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Why do I have to tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can, Witness, then answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that during the conflict, you were also fulltime employed.

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to your house in which you lived, how far was your workplace from it?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: It was far. In the shopping centre. I had to go there on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, that 1992, 1993, 1994, how often did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Every day. Every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to work, you said that you went every day. Did you use some means of transportation or did you walk or did you go on foot?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: On foot. Oh, dear, was it hard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if at the time when you went to work, and you tell us you did so every day, in the part of the town you lived in, would you used to see and come across soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't. No soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time when you would go to work or come back, can you tell us at what time did you go to work and at what time did you come back?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Early in the morning, and I'd come back in the evening. Early while it's still dark you go there and...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the institution that you worked for, Medresa, what is it?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: It is a religious establishment. You know what a religious establishment is, believers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when going to your place of work and on your way back, would you come across armed men enroute?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, because I went while it was still dark, and I would come back when it was dark again. So I didn't meet them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, when you went to work and returned from work, meet during that time, in 1992, 1993, and 1994, uniformed policemen, an armed soldier?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if during the conflict between 1992 and 1994, if your so was employed?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Was he employed? Yes, he was all the time, because he was a poor student so he couldn't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter makes a correction.

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I said he was poor, so he couldn't go to the front line. He had to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that his eyesight is poor, what do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I mean that he couldn't join the army, our defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us that your son was a soldier?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. I'm saying that they wanted him, but he couldn't because of his eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that because your son had some problems with his eyes, that he could not join the army for that reason?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in Sedrenik where were the positions of the army Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which called up your son? Can you tell us what was the name of that army?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know. How can I know that? I mean, defending his -- defending its people, they called them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that your son could not go to the front line, can you tell us in relation to your house in which you lived, where was that front line?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: You mean further away from my home?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far was it?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Are you asking me about Stijena?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the front line," he couldn't go to the front line, do you have any knowledge about Spicasta Stijena and Pasino Brdo which you mentioned? Were there any front lines in that part?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Above Pasino Brdo, there was our front line. That's what I heard when people talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And in relation to Spicasta Stijena, did you have any knowledge or did you hear where the front lines were of the army which called up your son, which you say defended?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in relation to your house, how far away from your house is Spicasta Stijena? It is a kilometre or what?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know. 500 -- no, little bit more. I don't really know. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe --

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know this. I can't write that down or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask you to pause between the answer and the new question to be put to the witness. Mrs. Ocuz, since whatever you say is translated, we are trying to slow down a bit in order to give the interpreters the opportunity to translate what you've said. So we're trying to slow down a bit. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm very upset. You understand, I'm very excited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... But this Court is very interested to hear what you say, and therefore translation is important. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, my last question was if you can describe to us the part about which you say is called Spicasta Stijena, what does it look like?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, it looks like a rock, like a hillock, like a hill, and those boulders there, and in front of them are houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And in that part where you told us where those boulders or a boulder --

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, boulders, boulder, a rock, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that part where that rock is, is it forested? Was there any forest there?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: There used to be. Yes, there used to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "there used to be," can you tell us, it was when? In what period, 1992, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, there is still the forest where it was, and as it is, nobody laid a finger on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that part where Spicasta Stijena is and you tell us there was some woods there, some forest, are you aware of the area called seven woods, Sedam Suma?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Why, yes, that's where we went to collect firewood.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That part which you tell us is called Sedam Suma, how far is it from your house?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. A bit further than Spicasta Stijena. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge or did you perhaps hear that in that part about which we have established right now is called Sedam Suma, if there were any troops there?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any troops there or what the place is called. I know where I went to collect firewood, Pasino Brdo, Sedam Suma.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often did you go to Pasino Brdo to fetch firewood?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, often. Every three nights or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Today, when asked by my learned friend, page 26, you said that you would spend the whole day and night in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no. At night. Not at night, I worked. By daytime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we apologise. My co-counsel tells me it is page 76. My apologies. Line 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to say that I went to work in daytime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone noticed that it must have been a mistake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us, what is true? Is it true that you went to work every day?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Every day I went to work, and then I come back. Then whatever my husband needs, I tend to my husband, prepare food for the next day, and then I work, all that I had to do. I've already told you, and then all over again. Go to work while it's still dark, and then when the night falls, and then go back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So it means that you are not right when you said that you were in the cellar all day?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes I was because when I went to work, it was the cellar. That is the cellar, because we worked in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And whilst you were at your workplace, was your son also full time and did he go to work?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where is it that he went to work?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: To Granap, to the city, to Granap.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how did he go to the city?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: On foot. We would go together and we would come back together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that you often went with your neighbour Mejra to collect firewood.

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the incident which happened which befell Mrs. Mejra when she was with you?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: When the fog started lifting, we hurried up, and I had run up to cover behind their house. And she had not made it yet. And a bullet targeted her, but she wasn't hit. I was scared but she said no, no, no, it only grazed me. And...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you could not remember the date.

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in relation to the incident about which you told us befell you on the 7th of October, 1993, was that before this incident which befell you or after it?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Before, before, before that thing with Mejra. No, no, no, it happened to Mejra before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, that day when you were out with Mejra, was there any gunfire in that area, in that part of Pasino Brdo where you were?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No. I don't know, I don't know. I don't know where this bullet came from. Wherever it could have come from, whether from Spicesta or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you told us that you went to look for firewood often in the direction of Pasino Brdo and Sedam Suma, did you, perhaps, hear that the gunfire came from that direction?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Sure I heard. We are collecting those -- this firewood, and then we hear a burst of fire, and then we get down to the ground and then start doing it again. And then there comes another, and then we are again prostate on the ground, and then collect a little bit more and then take to our heels and get back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we hear a burst of fire" could you determine by the sound -- since you are on a hill, could you determine the direction from which this burst was coming from?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: From Spicasta Stijena where we were -- to where we went to collect wood.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to Pasino Brdo where you were to get wood, how far is Spicasta Stijena from it?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know that. I don't know, 300 metres, something like that. But we pluck up the courage, let's go, let's get it. It's nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that -- you said that you knew that they were soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska where Spicasta Stijena is. Can you tell us how did you acquire that information? Did you see the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I saw them one night at 10.00. I heard some quarrel, some argument, and I looked and I saw two. What they were talking about, I don't know. Only I heard the noise, and I could hear how the two of them were quarrelling. I couldn't make out what it was about. I couldn't understand what they were saying, but I could see them arguing, and I tried to look at them through the binoculars, and then I said, forget the binoculars, I won't look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us you saw two men. What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: They had those rifles over their shoulders, and one had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Pasino Brdo to collect firewood, would you see soldiers of the BH army there?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, during the conflict in 1992, 1993, 1994, in the part of the city that you lived in, did you ever come across soldiers wearing olive-green uniforms with weapons?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, I did not see a thing. No troops. Yes, women, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you came across women. Can you tell us where were men?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, I also met men and women, but civilians. You don't know who they are, where they are, what they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could I just ask you how much time you need. I'm not quite sure whether this courtroom will be used this afternoon. I notice that you are approximately four or five minutes the examination-in-chief took. Madam Registrar, do you know if the courtroom will be used this afternoon? So if you would keep within your time limits, and I know it has been very long already for the interpreters. But if you would be able to finish in a couple of minutes, I'd like to know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Ocuz, can you tell us, in relation to your house, how far from it is your neighbour Mejra's house?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know. Not far. Not far. I don't know. I never measured it. How can I know it? All I know is that it's not far.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, you said that a sniper fired from Spicasta Stijena. Can you tell us what is a sniper?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: How do I know? It's a soldier. A sniper. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did your husband and your son have a rifle or some other weapon in the house?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, believe me, because they were not -- they were not prepared. I suppose they would have been given some, they would have been called up, I guess, if they were prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if your house is on the street, Sedrenik, or is it off the street?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: It's on Sedrenik Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if there were some shelters, some protection, against the snipers?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Only some sacks, some bags, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, apart from that occasion when your house was fired at as you tell us on that 7th of October, 1993, did you hear whether there was any gunfire in that part of the town that day?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I wasn't asking. I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what time of the day was it when it happened to you? You said lunchtime, but...

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, lunchtime, afternoon, 5.00, 4.00. Because my son came and said -- friend came to say that dad was not well so will you come home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that day you had gone to work and you had to come back from work?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: That's right. I had to return earlier because my friend had come to my -- had gone to my son in the shop and told him, "go and find your mother by whatever means you can and tell her that your dad is feeling bad." So a doctor came and they took him to the hospital, and he was given some medicines, and then we returned home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that that day when it happened to you, that that day you had returned home earlier and that your husband was then taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what time -- you say that it happened to you around 1700. When was your husband taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what time it was. Well, as soon as I came back, and I came back earlier. And then I said -- I took him to the hospital and sat down to have lunch with my son. And my neighbour took me back in the car. My son locked up the shop, and the neighbour said "I'll drive you. You can't walk." And because we were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you only -- only one more question. In the part of Sedrenik, of that neighbourhood where you lived, could you see any trenches there?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no, no. I didn't see any military trenches. I only saw those gullies which were made for us when we went to get the wood. That is all that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you think that there is a difference between trenches and gullies?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: Well, I think there is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the vicinity of these gullies or when you walked by, did you ever see any troops there?

utterances.speaker: NAZIJA OCUZ
utterances.text: No, no, no. Never. We only saw them next to Pasino Brdo. That is where we went for firewood, so if the fire starts, then we just take cover in those gullies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, is there any need to re-examine the witness? I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no further questions. Mrs. Ocuz, it might have taken you a lot of courage to come to The Hague. Perhaps an airplane was quite --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My heart aches. My soul aches. But I came because I know what is in my head and in my heart. And what I remember and what I know, I will smart from it to the end of my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that it must be very difficult for you because all the events of those days are very emotional to you. We fully understand that. And therefore, we specifically thank you for having come to The Hague, having answered all the questions the parties have put to you, for taking the courage to do all this. You well understand, it's very important for a Court to hear from witnesses who have been present at the days and the places where the conflict happened, to hear from them what it actually was. So I once again would like to thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I hope you have a safe trip home again. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I am taking this as a souvenir, as a souvenir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, would you please lead the witness, then, out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately we have no final information yet from the detention unit as to what will happen tomorrow morning. I therefore would like to ask the parties to be prepared tomorrow to continue. If possible, of course we'll finish the cross-examination of Mrs. Jusovic. I want to add in that respect that we've seen that she is rather vulnerable, she is fragile at this moment, and I would like you to keep this specifically in mind whenever it will come to a continuation of the cross-examination tomorrow morning. If not, we'll see what we'll do. If there are any witnesses, it will depend on the presence of General Galic we can proceed or not. But before we adjourn, first we have to take decisions as far as the admission of evidence is concerned. I think we have just one document, Madam Registrar. Would you please guide us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
